findings.title: Date-override days bypass the busy-time check entirely
findings.body: In `checkIfIsAvailable`, after the date-override block, `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` returns early, before `busy.every(...)` is evaluated. This means that for any slot on a day that has a date override, existing Cal bookings and external-calendar busy times for that host are completely ignored, so already-booked slots are reported as available. Since every non-round-robin host is treated as `isFixed`, this applies to personal and collective events too, and leads to double bookings on any day with a date override. The override result must be combined with the busy check instead of short-circuiting it.

findings.title: Working-hours check rejects slots when a host has multiple availability windows on the same day
findings.body: The new check uses `workingHours.find((workingHour) => { ... if (start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime) return true; })` and treats a truthy result as "slot is outside of working hours" -> unavailable. `getUserAvailability` returns one working-hours entry per availability row, so a user with a split schedule (e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00 on the same weekday) has two entries for that day. A 10:00 slot is inside the first entry but outside the second, so `find` matches the second entry and the slot is dropped. The logic must be `!workingHours.some(entry => slot is inside entry)` (i.e. unavailable only if no entry contains the slot). As written, availability is silently broken for every user with more than one availability window per day.

findings.title: `end` is computed from the slot start, not the slot end
findings.body: `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` duplicates the `start` computation on the previous line; it was clearly meant to be derived from `slotEndTime`. As a result the `end > workingHour.endTime` condition never considers the event length, so a slot that starts inside working hours but ends after them is not detected by this check.

findings.title: Date-override check rejects slots when a host has several ranges on the same date
findings.body: `dateOverrides.find((date) => { ... })` returns truthy as soon as *one* override range on the slot's date does not contain the slot, and the code then returns `false` ("slot is not within the date override"). A date override may legitimately contain multiple time ranges for the same date (e.g. 09:00-11:00 and 14:00-16:00). A slot inside the first range is outside the second, so it is incorrectly marked unavailable. The predicate must be inverted to "no range on that date contains the slot".

findings.title: Dayjs objects compared with `===`, condition is dead code
findings.body: `if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly created Dayjs objects by reference, which is never true. The intended check (a zero-length override, i.e. the organizer marked the day unavailable) therefore never executes. Use `.isSame(...)` or compare `valueOf()`.

findings.title: Override date compared in server-local time against a UTC slot time
findings.body: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` formats in the process's local timezone, while `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` is UTC (`time.utc()`). On a deployment whose system timezone is not UTC, the two date strings can differ for the same instant, so overrides are matched to the wrong day (or not matched at all), making the whole override branch behave differently per server timezone. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` for the comparison.

findings.title: Override end check ignores event length, allowing bookings that overrun the override
findings.body: `if (slotStartTime.isAfter(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")))` only tests the slot's *start* against the override end. For an override of 14:00-15:00 and a 60-minute event, a slot starting at 14:30 ends at 15:30 but is still considered inside the override and returned as available. Since for fixed hosts in round-robin events this is the only check against that host's override window, the fixed host can be booked outside their declared override. The comparison should use `slotEndTime`.

findings.title: Override timeZone is optional; dayjs .tz(undefined) silently falls back to the default timezone
findings.body: `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` is called with `override.timeZone` typed as optional (`timeZone?: string` in packages/types/schedule.d.ts). Any caller of `getSlots` that passes date overrides without a `timeZone` (the field is newly added, so existing callers do not set it) will have `.tz(undefined)` resolve to dayjs's default/guessed timezone, producing a wrong `organizerUtcOffset` and shifting the override by an arbitrary amount. Either make the field required on this code path or explicitly fall back to a known timezone (e.g. UTC) when it is missing.

findings.title: Timezone-shifted override wraps around midnight and lands on the wrong day
findings.body: `startTime`/`endTime` are computed as `hour() * 60 + minute()` of the offset-shifted override time, i.e. minutes since the invitee's midnight. When the shift pushes the override across a day boundary the day information is lost: e.g. an organizer override 09:00-11:00 in UTC+5:30 viewed by an invitee in UTC-8 shifts to 19:30-21:30 of the *previous* day, but is emitted as minutes 1170-1290 of the invitee's current day, so slots are offered at a completely wrong time. Negative/over-1440 minute offsets need to be handled (clip to the day or split across days), as `buildSlots` only understands minutes within the invitee day.

findings.title: No test for the PR's main fix (fixed-host date overrides in round-robin)
findings.body: The PR's primary change is that date overrides of fixed hosts are now honoured for ROUND_ROBIN events (via the new `dateOverrides`/`workingHours` handling in `checkIfIsAvailable`), but the only test added covers invitee-timezone handling for a single personal event. There is no test with a round-robin event type where a fixed host has a date override and the round-robin host does not, which is exactly the regression-prone path (and the path where the `dateOverrideExist -> return true` short-circuit and the split-working-hours bug manifest). Please add a getSchedule test for that scenario, including a host with multiple availability windows on the override day.

findings.title: toHaveTimeSlots matcher cannot detect missing slots
findings.body: The matcher iterates with `.every()` over the *actual* slots and compares them index-wise to `expectedSlots`, without comparing array lengths. If the implementation returns fewer slots than expected (e.g. the first N are correct but trailing slots are dropped), the assertion still passes. The newly added timezone assertion relies on this matcher, so a partial regression in override handling would go unnoticed; the matcher should also assert `schedule.slots[dateString].length === expectedSlots.length`.
